questions.question: Explain how acid rain forms and how it speeds up weathering, with reference to South Africa.
questions.expected_answer: Burning coal, oil and petrol releases sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, which form sulphuric and nitric acids that fall as acid rain/deposition. Natural rain pH about 5,6; acid rain below 5 (each unit lower is 10 times more acidic). It dissolves limestone and marble (calcium carbonate, crusts of gypsum), corrodes metals, damages paint, acidifies soils and lakes. South Africa relies on coal; Mpumalanga Highveld power stations and Secunda - Highveld Priority Area (2007); winds carry pollution far. Solutions: scrubbers, cleaner fuels, renewables.

questions.question: Describe how mining, quarrying and construction speed up weathering, including acid mine drainage.
questions.expected_answer: Exposing and blasting fresh rock creates cracks; water, frost and air attack it; rockfalls on road cuttings. Crushed waste rock and tailings have a large surface area and weather quickly. Witwatersrand gold mines (since 1886): pyrite oxidises in dumps and flooded tunnels, forming sulphuric acid and dissolving metals; after pumping stopped, acidic water decants into rivers and groundwater; treated by pumping and neutralising with lime. Also coal mines in Mpumalanga.

questions.question: Explain how agriculture, vegetation clearing and careless visitors affect weathering, and suggest ways to reduce human-caused weathering.
questions.expected_answer: Clearing vegetation exposes rock to heating/cooling and rain; ploughing exposes material; some fertilisers acidify soils; irrigation in dry areas causes salinisation and salt weathering (e.g. lower Orange River); cities - pollution, soot, heat island. Visitors wetting, touching, fires and graffiti damage San rock art (uKhahlamba-Drakensberg). Reduce: cleaner energy, emission standards, rehabilitating dumps and treating water, protecting vegetation, careful irrigation, drainage and maintenance of buildings, guided visits and never touching/wetting rock art (protected by law).
